speaker: Interviewer
text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Mostly rainy day and future plans, if I’m being honest. I’m not anywhere near buying a home yet, so over the last year I’ve been trying to build up an emergency cushion and also set aside a little for bigger goals down the line. I’ve been pretty focused on saving for a car repair fund, unexpected bills, and eventually classes for hospitality or a manager certification.

I also keep a small separate bucket for things I actually enjoy, like a weekend trip up to Door County or tickets for a Brewers game, but I’m pretty careful about that. I like knowing I’ve got a buffer more than spending just to spend.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it’s been like for you living here.

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Living in Madison has been a pretty good fit for me overall. I like that it feels manageable—big enough that there’s always something going on, but not so huge that everything feels hectic all the time. I’ve lived here my whole life, so there’s a comfort to it. I know the neighborhoods, I know the routines, I know where to get decent produce, where to go for a run, all that stuff.

One of the biggest upsides is the balance. You can work hard during the week and still have access to lakes, parks, farmers markets, local events, and good food without needing to turn everything into some big expensive production. I like being able to run around Lake Mendota, hit a local art walk once in a while, or just keep things simple and meet up with friends for a beer and some curds. It feels grounded here.

The downside is that the cost of living has definitely gotten harder to ignore. Even if you’re careful, rent, groceries, gas—everything adds up. Winters can also be rough. I’m used to them, but there are definitely stretches where it feels gray forever and you’re just trying to get through to spring. And because I’ve been here so long, sometimes I do get that feeling of wanting to branch out a little more, even just for a change of pace.

But overall, I’d say Madison gives me stability, and I value that a lot. It feels like a place where you can build toward something if you stay disciplined.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Yeah, I’d say there was.

A few years ago, I was at a point where I had to decide whether I was going to keep drifting from job to job a little bit, or actually treat work like something I could build a future around. It wasn’t some dramatic movie moment, but it mattered a lot to me.

After high school, I mostly did what a lot of people do when they’re not totally sure of the long-term plan. I worked, helped out where I could, tried to stay responsible, paid my bills, and told myself I’d figure it out as I went. I had a couple different service jobs, and I kept thinking maybe eventually I’d go back to school full-time or maybe some better opportunity would just kind of appear. But I wasn’t really moving toward anything specific. I was working hard, but not with a clear direction.

Then there was a stretch where money got tight all at once. Nothing catastrophic, just real-life stuff stacking up—rent, car issues, higher grocery costs, and that feeling of looking at your account and realizing there’s zero room for mistakes. Around the same time, at work, I started noticing that I was already acting like the person people relied on. I was the one double-checking the drawer, catching little inventory mistakes, helping train newer people, staying calm when the line got long or a customer came in upset. And I remember thinking, if I’m already carrying myself this way, why am I still thinking of this like it’s temporary?

That was kind of the crossroads.

One path was to keep treating work as just something to get through while waiting for my “real” future to start. The other was to admit that I’m actually good at operations, good with customers under pressure, good at keeping things organized, and that there’s nothing small about building a stable career from that. Once I really accepted that, my mindset changed.

So I started getting a lot more intentional. I got stricter about budgeting. I started saving with actual categories instead of just hoping there’d be money left over. I paid more attention to how shifts were run, how managers handled labor and inventory, what made one day smooth and another one a mess. I started thinking in terms of, what would I do if I were the shift supervisor? What would I improve? How do I make myself the obvious choice when that opportunity comes up?

That choice changed me because it gave me direction. I stopped feeling embarrassed that my path didn’t look flashy. I started feeling proud that I’m dependable, that I can handle pressure, that I know how to make things run. It also made me more disciplined outside of work. I got even more into planning, routines, saving, keeping my life organized—basically building a foundation instead of just reacting.

And I think the ending of that story is still being written, honestly. I haven’t hit every goal yet. I’m still working toward the promotion, still want to do the hospitality classes and get certified, still want to save enough to have more options. But that was the moment that really defined who I am now—when I stopped waiting for a different life to start and decided to take my own work and ambition seriously.

speaker: Interviewer
text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?

speaker: Interviewee
text: Right now I live with one roommate in Madison. We mostly keep to our own routines, and it helps keep costs a little more manageable.

speaker: Interviewer
text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?

speaker: Interviewee
text:
It was a food service place—fast, customer-facing, pretty high-volume. The kind of place where you’re handling orders nonstop, working the register, keeping the line moving, and making sure food gets out right and on time.

So the business was basically selling prepared food and drinks to people who wanted something quick, affordable, and consistent. A lot of the work behind the scenes was making sure the kitchen stayed stocked, prep was done right, food safety rules were followed, and the front counter didn’t fall apart when it got busy. It wasn’t glamorous, but it took a lot of coordination to keep everything running smoothly.

speaker: Interviewer
text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?

speaker: Interviewee
text:
I work in fast food and counter service, mostly front-of-house but really a little bit of everything depending on the shift. A typical day for me means running the register, taking orders, handling cash, helping with drinks and bagging, keeping the area stocked and clean, and jumping in to fix little problems before they turn into bigger ones. When it gets busy, it’s a lot of multitasking and keeping calm so the whole line doesn’t back up.

My schedule moves around some, which is pretty normal in this kind of work. I usually work a mix of weekday shifts and some weekends, and I’ve done both mornings and later shifts depending on what’s needed. A lot of times it’s the rush periods—breakfast, lunch, or early dinner—when things are busiest, so those are the hours they really need people who can stay organized and move fast.

speaker: Interviewer
text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Last month, my household probably spent around $2,300 to $2,600 total, and that’s pretty close to a normal month for me, give or take if something annoying comes up like car maintenance or a higher utility bill.

My biggest share is rent and utilities. With a roommate, my portion is a lot more manageable than living alone, but that still takes the biggest chunk. After that it’s groceries, gas, phone, car insurance, and the usual household basics like cleaning supplies and toiletries. I also spend on eating out here and there, but I try to keep that pretty controlled since I already work in food service and know how fast little purchases add up.

A more typical breakdown for my part would be something like:
- Rent: around $750
- Utilities/internet: around $150 to $200
- Groceries: around $250 to $300
- Gas: around $120 to $160
- Car insurance: around $110
- Phone: around $70
- Household items/miscellaneous: maybe $100 to $150
- Eating out or small fun stuff: maybe $100 to $150

If it’s not a usual month, it’s usually because of seasonal stuff—higher heating costs in winter, more driving, or something like a car repair. I try to keep my spending pretty steady and track it closely so I’m not surprised at the end of the month.

speaker: Interviewer
text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?

speaker: Interviewee
text: Yes, I did. I worked my regular shifts this past week.

speaker: Interviewer
text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Overall, pretty solid. In this kind of job, your shift can go sideways fast if people don’t communicate well, so I really value coworkers who show up, stay on task, and don’t make everything more complicated than it needs to be.

With my manager, I’d say the relationship is respectful and pretty practical. I’m not someone who needs a lot of hand-holding, and I think they know I’m dependable. If I’m asked to cover something, train someone new, or keep an eye on the front when it gets hectic, I usually do it without a lot of drama. I pay attention, I try to stay organized, and I think that’s earned me some trust. Like any workplace, there are moments where schedules change last minute or decisions get made that are frustrating, but I try to handle that professionally instead of taking everything personally.

With coworkers, it’s a mix, but mostly good. I get along best with people who are reliable and work with some urgency, especially during a rush. We don’t have to be best friends, but I do think mutual respect matters a lot. I’m usually the kind of person who will step in, answer questions, or help keep things moving if someone is overwhelmed. At the same time, I can get frustrated by people who are careless, show up late all the time, or leave things for the next person to fix. In food service, that kind of stuff affects everybody.

So I’d say my relationships at work are positive, but grounded. I’m friendly, I’m team-oriented, and I want the shift to run well. I think people know I care about doing things right.

speaker: Interviewer
text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?

speaker: Interviewee
text:
I think about it mostly in terms of fairness, accountability, and whether people are actually being treated with the same dignity and protection. To me, the issues Black Lives Matter raises aren’t abstract—they’re about whether someone can move through daily life, work, drive, shop, or ask for help without being treated like a threat first.

I’m not someone who wants to speak like I know everything, because I don’t. But I do think the movement pushed a lot of people, including me, to pay closer attention to things that were easy for some of us to not think about enough before—especially policing, unequal treatment, and how race affects people’s opportunities and sense of safety.

I was raised to believe in hard work, respect, and community, and part of that for me is being honest that not everyone gets treated equally, even if they’re doing everything right. I think that deserves to be taken seriously, not brushed off or turned into a talking point.

At the same time, I’m pretty practical by nature, so I also think a lot about what actually helps—better accountability, better training, listening to people’s experiences, and trying to make systems more fair instead of just arguing in circles. Mostly I’ve been thinking that it’s important to pay attention, keep learning, and not get defensive when people are talking about real problems.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?

speaker: Interviewee
text: Yes, I was born in the United States. I was born and raised in Madison, Wisconsin.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?

speaker: Interviewee
text: Just one job in the past month. My regular fast food/counter service job.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Now we’d like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Overall, I’d say my health is pretty decent. I’m not dealing with any major medical issues, and I try to stay on top of the basics because if I let things slide, I feel it fast—especially with the kind of work I do. Being on your feet for long shifts, moving constantly, dealing with stress, that all adds up.

I try to keep active pretty regularly. I run a few miles around Lake Mendota when I can, usually a few times a week if my schedule cooperates, and that helps me a lot with both fitness and stress. I’m not some extreme athlete, but I like having a routine and feeling like my stamina is good. Work itself is also pretty physical, so I’m moving around a lot even on days I don’t formally exercise.

Food-wise, I try to do reasonably well. I’m around fast food all the time, so I have to be intentional or it gets too easy to just grab whatever’s convenient. I cook at home a fair amount, and that helps. I’m not perfect about it, but I try to keep things balanced—real meals, decent portions, not overdoing it. I also garden a little, so in season I like using my own tomatoes and herbs, which makes me feel a little more on track.

If I’m honest, the bigger health challenge for me is stress and fatigue more than anything dramatic. Weird schedules, busy shifts, money worries, and just regular life stuff can wear you down. I do pretty well when I stick to routines—sleep, meal prep, running, planning things out. When my schedule gets chaotic, that’s usually when I feel less healthy, even if nothing is technically wrong.

Mentally, I’d say I’m generally steady, but I definitely need structure. I’m the kind of person who feels better when things are organized and I know what the week looks like. Writing things down, budgeting, journaling, and keeping routines actually helps my stress a lot.

So overall: decent health, active, able to work, trying to be responsible about it, but like a lot of people, I’m balancing physical health with stress, sleep, and keeping life manageable.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain – anything like that.

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Nothing major, thankfully. In the past two years I haven’t had any big diagnosis, broken bones, or anything that took me out of work for a long time.

It’s been more minor, everyday stuff than anything serious. I’ve had periods of foot and lower back soreness from being on my feet so much at work, especially during stretches with a lot of long shifts. I’ve also had some muscle tightness or soreness from running if I push it and don’t recover well. Usually that’s the kind of thing I handle with better shoes, stretching, rest, and being a little more disciplined about not overdoing it.

The bigger pattern has honestly been stress and fatigue. When my schedule gets messy or I’m not sleeping enough, I feel run down pretty quickly. There have been times where I’ve felt burned out or had headaches more often, but not in a way that turned into some major medical event.

So overall, no big health crisis—just the wear-and-tear kind of stuff, plus stress, that I try to stay on top of before it becomes a bigger problem.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven’t had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Yeah, there have definitely been moments like that in the past year. I’ve managed to keep the major bills paid, but there were a few stretches where it felt way too close for comfort.

The biggest situations were usually around unexpected expenses—car stuff, higher utility bills in winter, or groceries jumping up when I was already trying to stretch things. I remember at least a couple times where I had to really reshuffle everything, put off buying something I needed, or wait until my next paycheck. Nothing extravagant either—more like delaying routine things, replacing shoes later than I should have, putting off a non-urgent appointment, or cutting back hard on groceries and fun spending so I could cover rent and essentials.

There’s also been that feeling of looking at a bill and knowing I can pay it, but only if I pull money from what I was trying to save for emergencies or future plans. To me that still counts, because it means there really wasn’t enough room in the budget.

So I wouldn’t say I was completely unable to survive or that I missed everything, but yes, there were definitely times this past year when money was tight enough that I had to delay needed purchases and scramble to make bills work.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Yeah, they definitely move around over the year, even if I try hard to keep things predictable.

Utilities are probably the clearest example. In winter, heating costs go up, and that can make the monthly total feel pretty different from a milder month. Summer’s usually a little easier, unless it’s really hot and the electric bill bumps up from fans or AC. So even if rent stays the same, that utilities piece isn’t fixed.

Groceries have fluctuated a lot too, mostly just because prices have been all over the place. Some months I can keep that pretty controlled if I’m meal prepping, buying basics, and using stuff from my garden in season. Other months it feels like the same cart costs noticeably more, especially if I need household items at the same time.

Gas changes depending on both prices and how much I’m driving. If I’m just doing my normal work commute and errands, it’s one thing. If I’m covering more shifts, driving more in bad weather, or making a weekend trip, that goes up fast. Car-related costs are the ones that can really throw everything off, though—oil changes, new tires, brake work, whatever decides to happen at the worst time.

Then there are the smaller seasonal or occasional expenses. Around the holidays, spending usually goes up some even if I try to keep it modest—gifts, food, family stuff, maybe a little extra travel. In colder months I also end up spending more on things like winter gear, replacing boots, or just trying to keep up with weather-related stuff. And every so often there’s a month where you need to restock basics all at once—cleaning supplies, toiletries, pantry items—and it feels bigger than usual.

So the pattern is basically: fixed core bills, but a lot of variation around utilities, groceries, gas, and surprise car or seasonal costs. That’s why I try to budget a little cautiously, because one “normal” month can turn into a more expensive one pretty quickly.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you’re paying on right now.

speaker: Interviewee
text:
Right now I don’t have student loans, which I’m grateful for. The main debt I’m paying on is credit card debt, and I try to stay pretty disciplined about it. It’s not massive, but it’s the kind of balance that built up from regular life stuff more than anything flashy—car repairs, higher everyday costs, a few months where bills hit all at once, that kind of thing.

I usually try to pay more than the minimum whenever I can, because I hate carrying a balance and watching interest eat away at my money. Some months I make decent progress, and other months I’m just trying not to add to it. I’ve also had to use the card at times as a buffer when cash flow got tight, which I don’t love, but that’s been the reality here and there.

Other than that, I have the usual monthly obligations like car insurance, phone, rent, and utilities, but I don’t really think of those as debt unless I’m behind, and I’ve tried hard to avoid that. I’m not currently paying back family or friends, and I don’t have a personal loan or anything like that.

So overall: mostly some credit card debt, managed carefully, and a strong preference to get it down so I’ve got more breathing room.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?

speaker: Interviewee
text: I’ve never been married, and no, I’m not living with a romantic partner right now. I live with one roommate.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Now we’d like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?

speaker: Interviewee
text:
My biggest expenses last month were definitely the basics first. Rent was the biggest one, around $750 for my share, and then utilities and internet on top of that—probably another $150 to $200 total depending on the month.

After housing, groceries were a big expense, around $250 to $300. I try to be careful there, but food prices add up fast even when you’re planning. Gas was another noticeable one, probably around $120 to $160, since I need my car for work and regular errands.

Then there were the fixed bills: car insurance, about $110, and my phone bill, around $70. I also had the usual smaller but necessary stuff like household supplies, toiletries, and a little bit of credit card payment, which all count even if they don’t feel as dramatic one by one.

So overall, the biggest expenses were housing first, then groceries, transportation, and the regular monthly bills.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away – traveling, at school, or in a hospital?

speaker: Interviewee
text: No, it’s just me and my roommate right now. No one who usually lives here is away.

speaker: Interviewer
text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?

speaker: Interviewee
text: My roommate and I share the household expenses. We split the rent and most of the basic shared bills like utilities and internet. Then we each cover our own personal stuff separately, like our phone bills, car expenses, groceries when we buy our own food, and anything individual like that.
